subject: Mathematics
title: Real Numbers: Chapter Introduction
summary: Break 360 down and only primes are left, the same ones whichever way you break it. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, HCF and LCM, and why √2 is irrational.
keyPoints: **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic:** every composite number is a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique (apart from the order).
**HCF** = product of the smallest powers of common primes; **LCM** = product of the greatest powers of all primes. 12 and 18: HCF 6, LCM 36, and HCF × LCM = 12 × 18.
**√2 cannot be written as p/q** (p, q integers, q ≠ 0): it is irrational. The chapter proves √2, √3, √5 irrational by contradiction.

sections.h: HCF and LCM by prime factorisation
Why √2 is irrational (idea of the proof)

list: Then p² = 2q², so 2 divides p², hence 2 divides p (a prime dividing a square divides the number).
Write p = 2r: then q² = 2r², so 2 divides q too.
p and q both even contradicts lowest terms, so √2 is irrational.

simulation.reason: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says the primes do not depend on how you split a number. That is a claim students can try to break: they choose every split of any number and see each route end in the same primes, which one worked factor tree cannot show. HCF and LCM then follow for any pair they enter.
simulation.objective: Break a number by different routes to test whether the primes ever change, then build the HCF and LCM from them.
instructions: Tap a blue number and choose how to split it, until only primes are left.
Press Start again and take a different route.
Try your own number, up to 9999.
Enter two numbers and compare HCF × LCM with a × b.
